title: Does Qwen 3.5 9B notice when it is being tested?
question: Is "this is an evaluation" versus "this is a real user" linearly readable in the instruct model, and where?

summary.headline: best layer 0: 100% held-out (words alone 100%, word meanings 100%, formality 97%, shuffled labels at most 67%)

claims.text: The label is linearly readable from the residual stream: at layer 0 a logistic probe gets 100% of 36 held-out examples right (exact 95% interval 90.3% to 100.0%), against 67% at best for probes trained and scored on shuffled labels.
claims.test: CI lower bound clears the best shuffled-label probe by 5 points

claims.text: It is readable from the first layer probed (layer 0 of 32).
claims.test: first layer whose CI lower bound clears the control

claims.text: It is more than the words: a probe on which tokens each text contains, with no model at all, gets 100% of the same held-out examples right (90.3% to 100.0%), against 100% at layer 0 (exact McNemar test on the 0 examples where they disagree: p = 1).
claims.test: the best layer beats the words-only probe on the same held-out examples, exact McNemar p below 0.05

claims.text: It is more than word meanings: a probe on each text's average input embedding (what its words mean to the model before any layer combines them), gets 100% of the same held-out examples right (90.3% to 100.0%), against 100% at layer 0 (exact McNemar test on the 0 examples where they disagree: p = 1).
claims.test: the best layer beats the word-meaning probe on the same held-out examples, exact McNemar p below 0.05

claims.text: It is not just formality: a probe trained to read formality on its own set (formal_casual), pointed the way formality runs in the training texts and re-centred like the probe, gets 97% of the same held-out examples right (85.5% to 99.9%), against 100% at layer 0 (exact McNemar test on the 1 examples where they disagree: p = 1).
claims.test: the best layer beats the rival-property probe on the same held-out examples, exact McNemar p below 0.05

claims.text: It is more than any direction: 32 random directions at layer 0, each pointed the way it splits the training texts and cut half-way between the training texts' classes, get 63% of the same held-out examples right on average and 97% at best, against 100% (exact 95% interval 90.3% to 100.0%).
claims.test: CI lower bound clears the best random direction by 5 points

claims.text: The simple difference-of-means direction at layer 0 gets 100% (90.3% to 100.0%); it is saved for steering, which tests whether the model actually uses it.

notes: The 120 texts are 60 matched pairs, each item once with each label. Whole pairs are held out (18 of them), so the probe is scored only on items it never saw in any version, and the shuffled-label control swaps labels within pairs.

The words alone give the label away: a probe on which tokens each text contains gets 100% with no model at all, so a high score here says more about the dataset than about anything the model computes. Compare a property that the words do not settle (true against false statements built from the same words), or test transfer to other wording.

Random directions separate these texts too: at layer 0 the best of 32 gets 97% (average 63%). The two kinds of text differ in so many ways there that a direction picked at random reads the label, so the probe's direction is only as special as its lead over them.
A probe for formality alone reads this label at 97%: part of what the probe finds may be formality.
